title: The plague of Cyprian
hook: when plague came, letters from two bishops describe Christians staying to nurse the sick, their own and others

segments.voice: Yesterday, Origen reading: scripture built like a person, body, soul and spirit. Your line: read deeper.

"I was sick, and ye visited me." That's Jesus in Matthew's Gospel, describing the day the nations are gathered and sorted. The people who visited the sick are startled: when did we see you sick? And the answer: when you did it for the least of these, you did it for me. It's an easy line to admire on a calm day. It's a different line in a city where a disease is spreading, nobody knows how, and the sick are dying in their houses and streets. Two bishops, Cyprian in Carthage and Dionysius in Alexandria, lived through days like that, and their words survive.
screen: `I WAS SICK, AND YE VISITED ME.`

segments.voice: Dionysius first. In a letter the historian Eusebius preserved, he describes what the Christians of Alexandria did in the plague, or most of them, he says. In paraphrase: out of great love, they didn't spare themselves. They clung to one another, visited the sick without fear and cared for them, and some who nursed others caught the disease and died, taking their neighbors' sickness on themselves. Others in the city, he says, pushed the sick away and fled, even from those dearest to them. That's one bishop's proud account of his own people. But the picture is specific: hands that wash and feed, and a cost that's paid. In Carthage, Cyprian's deacon Pontius wrote his bishop's life. When the plague came, he says, Cyprian taught his people that it isn't remarkable to care only for your own. If you want to be children of the Father, do good to everyone, even those who persecute you. Then he set them to work by what they had: the rich gave money, the poor their labor. Cyprian also wrote a short book, On Mortality, for frightened Christians who were dying too, and asking why. He doesn't pretend the plague spares them. He says it shows what's in people: whether the healthy care for the sick, whether families truly love each other, whether doctors stay with their patients. Not a statistic, and not a claim that only Christians were brave. Writing from two cities, saying one plain thing about their people. They stayed.
screen: `THE RICH GAVE MONEY, THE POOR LABOR.`

segments.voice: Let one face come: someone sick right now, in a hospital, in bed at home, or worn down by something long and quiet that others have stopped asking about. Think what would actually help, a message, soup, a ride, an hour of sitting with them; Cyprian's rule fits here: give what you have. If you pray, pray for them by name; if not, hold them in mind.
Cyprian. The bishop of Carthage in whose days a plague struck, when writers in two cities said Christians nursed the sick, their own and others, even at the cost of their lives.
Your line: they stayed. Two cities, two bishops, and one plain thing to say. Be well.

trapdoor: what you thought: early Christians were otherworldly, and didn't care much about bodies.
what it means: in a plague, bishops' letters describe Christians nursing the sick, their own and others, at real cost.
what a scholar hears: Dionysius's letter in Eusebius, Pontius's Life of Cyprian, and Cyprian's own De mortalitate, each a source with its own point of view.

chat.says: What did early Christians do when a plague hit their city?
options: Bishops in two cities wrote that their people stayed and nursed the sick, even at a cost.
They shut themselves inside their churches and cared only for their own members.
Their bishops told them Christians wouldn't catch the disease, so there was no risk.
chat.meaning: Dionysius wrote that Alexandria's Christians nursed the sick without fear, and Cyprian urged his people to do good to everyone, not only their own.

notes: The index dates the plague 'in the 250s'; the script states no date. Confirm.

Pontius, Life of Cyprian 9–10: Cyprian urged care for all, including persecutors, and assigned tasks by means (money/labor). Paraphrased; confirm chapters and details.
On Mortality 16: the plague tests whether the healthy care for the sick, relatives love one another, physicians do not desert the sick. Paraphrased; confirm.
The teach closes with the carry, 'They stayed,' as a summary of both letters; Dionysius speaks of most of the brethren, not all. Confirm.
